title: The Cynic’s Guide to Church
text:
What this is
This is a class for people who have complicated, honest, unresolved feelings about the church.
Not a debate. Not a recovery program. Not Sunday school. Not a space where you’ll be told to forgive faster, doubt less, or look on the bright side.
It’s a space where you can name what you’ve experienced…the good and the bad…examine it honestly, and figure out what to do with it.
Over eight sessions, we’ll hold two things at the same time without letting either one cancel out the other:
Both are true. The goal is to wrestle with that tension in an honest way.

Who this is for
This class is for:

Current attenders who are struggling with aspects of their church experience
People who have stepped back or left and aren’t sure what to do next
Longtime churchgoers who feel disillusioned but can’t fully articulate why
Skeptics and returnees who are somewhere in between
Church lovers who are consistently lifted up by their church experience

You don’t have to have it figured out.

Before you begin
Read the Ground Rules before your first session. They’re not a list of restrictions — they’re the conditions that make honest conversation possible.

This class was built for a specific community, but the questions belong to anyone who has ever loved the church, been hurt by it, or both.

title: Ground Rules
text:
Why we make agreements together
Group norms are chosen, handed down, or emerge unconciously.
In this class, we want to chose our norms. The list below reflects a starting point, what seems to be common in most effective studies involving personal disclosure: “What do I need from this room in order to tell the truth?”
These are a starting point and we may add/delete in Session 1.

title: Ground Rules
text:
The covenant

The Cynic’s Guide to Church — Group Covenant

What is shared here stays here. What you learn about yourself is yours to take. Stories stay. Lessons leave. You can talk about what you’re learning. You should not talk outside this room about who said what.
You can share your experience without being the spokesperson for everyone who has had experiences like yours. You are not the representative of “all abuse survivors” or “all evangelicals” or “all people who left.” You speak only for yourself.
We are not here to fix everyone. We are here to understand each other. This is not a debate. The goal is listening and processing, not preparing our rebuttal while someone else is speaking.
You can pass. Always. On anything. Silence is participation. You do not have to share to be here. Nobody should feel pressure to disclose anything they’re not ready to share.
Speak from your own experience. Use “I” language. “I felt…” not “People like that always…” “In my experience…” not “The church never…”
Questions are welcome. You don’t have to resolve them to ask them. Sitting with a hard question is not the same as failing to answer it. Both belong here. If you feel uncomfortable discussing something in class, let me know. I promise you will not offend me.
The facilitator is not perfect. If you feel something is in error, you have 100% permission to bring it up. I, as your facilitator also reserve the right to say, “I don’t know”…a lot
Be as honest as you are able. Performative positivity — saying what you think you should feel — is as unhelpful here as unchecked venting. We want what is actually true for you.
Assume positive intent. Most people in this room are trying. When something lands wrong, say so — but assume accident before malice.
Be humble. There are multiple sides to any and everything.

title: Ground Rules
text:
A few words on confidentiality
Confidentiality is the most important agreement on this list, and it deserves more than a bullet point.
What confidentiality means here:

The specific things people share in this room: their stories, their pain, their doubts — stay in this room.
You may share with a spouse or close friend that you’re processing something, without naming what anyone else said.
No gossip. You may not share someone’s story as an anecdote. You may not use what you’ve heard here as data points in arguments elsewhere.

What confidentiality doesn’t mean:

1. Opening Exercise — What Do We Mean? (0:10–0:25)
Put these five sentences on a screen or whiteboard. Read each one aloud, then ask: “What does the word ‘church’ mean in this sentence?”






Tip




“Where do you go to church?”
“Church starts at 10.”
“We haven’t been to church lately.”
“That church has great preaching.”
“We’re looking for a church with a good youth program.”



Go through them one at a time. Let the group name what “church” is pointing to. They will notice that it means something different in almost every sentence — a place, an event, a habit, an organization, a service provider.






Note



🗒️ Facilitator note: Don’t correct anything yet. Just surface the range. Then say: “So when we say ‘the church has failed people’ or ‘the church changed my life’ — what are we actually talking about? Tonight we try to find out what the New Testament is pointing to when it uses this word.”

title: Session 2
section: 2. Teaching — Ekklēsia in the New Testament (0:25–0:55)
text:
2. Teaching — Ekklēsia in the New Testament (0:25–0:55)






Note



🗒️ Facilitator note: Keep each section to 5–8 minutes of talking. Pause for reactions. Never more than 10 consecutive minutes of you speaking. The goal is guided discovery, not lecture.



The word itself
The Greek word behind our English “church” is:

ἐκκλησία — ekklēsia (ek-klay-SEE-ah) Usually translated: church, assembly, congregation







Important



Key point: This word was not invented by Christians. It was ordinary Greek for an assembly of people. When a first-century Christian heard ekklēsia, their mental picture was not a building with pews and programs. It was: a people, an assembly, a gathered community.


There is also an interesting translation wrinkle: our English word “church” does not come from ekklēsia at all. It comes from kyriakon, meaning “belonging to the Lord.”



Language
Word
Root




English
church
kyriakon


Scottish
kirk

German
Kirche
kyriakon


English (academic)
ecclesiastical
ekklēsia



Knowing the Greek can correct some of the baggage we unconsciously attach to the English word.



How the New Testament uses ekklēsia



Use
Example
Meaning




Ordinary crowd
Acts 19:32
A pagan mob in confusion


Civic assembly
Acts 19:39
Official public gathering


Israel’s assembly
Acts 7:38
God’s OT people gathered


House church
Romans 16:5
Believers at Priscilla & Aquila’s home


City church
1 Cor. 1:2
All Christians in Corinth


Gathered meeting
1 Cor. 11:18

Universal church
Eph. 1:22–23
The whole body of Christ









Tip



Table exercise (5 min): In pairs, read Acts 19:32, 39, and 41. Is Luke saying “the church was in confusion”? What does this tell us about the word ekklēsia?





What Jesus said
Ekklēsia appears only in Matthew, twice:

Matthew 16:18 — “I will build my* ekklēsia.” Matthew 18:17 — “Tell it to the* ekklēsia.”

Two things matter here:

The possessive — Jesus says *“my* ekklēsia.” The church belongs to Christ, not to a denomination, building, or pastor.
The concreteness — In Matthew 18, the ekklēsia is a recognizable community that can hear a dispute and respond. This is not abstract theology. It is an actual group of people who know each other.







Important



The tension: The church is both a theological reality and a specific community of actual people. The New Testament holds both at once.





Acts shows us the people

“Saul began to destroy the church.” (Acts 8:3)

Saul was not destroying buildings. He was entering houses and dragging people away. So what was “the church” that Saul was attacking?
People.
Paul does not write “To Corinth Community Church.” He writes “To God’s ekklēsia that is in Corinth.” That is a subtle but significant difference.



One popular explanation that does not quite work
You have probably heard this:

“Ekklēsia comes from ek (out of) and kaleō (to call), so the church literally means ‘the called-out ones.’“

Do not teach it that way. Acts 19 disproves it — the pagan mob rioting in Ephesus is called an ekklēsia. Luke is not suggesting rioters are spiritually called-out ones. By the NT period, the word simply meant assembly.







✅ Accurate
❌ Not quite right




“God has called his people.”
“Ekklēsia literally means called-out ones.”


“Christians are called out of darkness.” (1 Pet. 2:9)
“The Greek proves the church is defined by being called out.”

title: Session 2
text:
3. Teaching — The Temple Connection (1:05–1:35)
The New Testament makes a stunning claim: the people do not go to a sacred place. The people become the sacred place.

The progression under the Old Covenant
God’s presence was associated with a place, structured around restricted access:
Tabernacle → Temple → Holy of Holies → Curtain
That architecture communicated: God is holy, humanity is estranged, access is restricted.
Then at Jesus’ death:

“The curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.” — Matthew 27:51

Hebrews makes the connection explicit: believers now have direct confidence to enter God’s presence through Christ (Hebrews 10:19–22).
So what happens to the sacred place?






Tip



Small group exercise (8 min): Divide into three groups. Each reads one passage and answers: “What does this say the church is? What would a community that actually believed this look like?“

Group 1: 1 Corinthians 3:16–17
Group 2: Ephesians 2:19–22
Group 3: 1 Peter 2:4–5

Report back.








Important



The New Testament does not replace a Jewish sacred building with a Christian sacred building. It does something far more radical: the people become the building.
God no longer primarily dwells among his people in a sacred structure. He dwells in his people by the Spirit.





Four images for the church









Image
Greek
Key text
What it communicates

ekklēsia
Matt. 16:18
A gathered people belonging to Christ


Body of Christ
sōma Christou
Eph. 1:22–23
Joined to Christ, joined to each other


Temple of God
naos theou
1 Cor. 3:16
God’s Spirit dwells in his people


Household of God
oikos theou
Eph. 2:19
Family, belonging, shared life






The reversals







Temple logic
Church logic




Concentric rings of access
Direct access for all through Christ


Priests mediate God’s presence
One mediator: Christ alone (1 Tim. 2:5)


Repeated sacrifice
One sacrifice, finished (Heb. 10:12)


World moves toward sacred center
Gospel moves outward into the world


National — gathered around Israel
International — all nations (Matt. 28:19)


Dividing wall: Jew / Gentile
Dividing wall destroyed (Eph. 2:14)






The biblical arc







Stage
Description




Eden
God with humanity


Tabernacle
God dwelling among Israel


Temple
God’s localized covenant presence


Jesus
“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”


Church
God’s Spirit dwelling in his people


New Creation
“The dwelling place of God is with man” (Rev. 21:3)









Note



🗒️ Facilitator note: Draw this timeline on a whiteboard slowly. Pause at each step. Ask: “So where does the church fit in this story?” Let them place it before you name it.


The church is an intermediate form appropriate to an intermediate age. We do not yet experience God’s presence as we will in the new creation — but neither are we standing behind the curtain waiting for access.



A challenging implication






Important



If that is right, then the way the church exists is supposed to communicate the gospel.
A church can verbally proclaim the priesthood of all believers while structurally making Christians into spectators. It can proclaim that God dwells in his people while functionally treating a building as the locus of God’s activity. It can proclaim reconciliation while organizing itself around demographic similarity. It can proclaim servanthood while creating celebrity leaders.
The question is not only: what does our church say? It is: what does our structure appear to say?

title: Session 2
text:
4. Discussion (1:35–1:50)


Before tonight, when you pictured “the church,” what did you picture? How does the ekklēsia material change that — if at all?
The New Testament says God’s Spirit dwells in his people. What would it mean to take that seriously? What would change about how you think about yourself?
The Temple had a curtain separating ordinary people from God’s presence. The gospel tears that curtain. Where have you experienced churches that put the curtain back up — making access to God feel restricted, conditional, or mediated through a leader?
This may open difficult territory. Hold it carefully.
Ephesians 2 says the church is supposed to embody reconciliation between people who were previously divided. Where have you seen that happen? Where have you seen churches reinforce those divisions instead?

title: Session 2
text:
Close (1:50–2:00)

“The New Testament’s picture of church is simpler and more radical than what most of us have experienced. It’s people — belonging to Christ, joined to each other, becoming the place where God’s presence lives in the world. Everything else we call ‘church’ is downstream from that.
Next week we ask: if that’s the purpose, what does the church actually need to do — and how did we get from people gathered in houses to organizations with staff, buildings, programs, and budgets? That turns out to be a really interesting story.”







Tip



Seed question for the week:
Think about a place or moment where you most clearly sensed God’s presence. Was it in a building? A gathering? A moment with one other person? What does your answer tell you about where you instinctively locate God’s presence — and how does that compare to what the New Testament describes?

title: Session 3
text:
Overview
Last session we established what “church” is in the New Testament. This session asks: what is it for, and how did we get from there to here?
Three moves:

A framework — Purpose, Functions, Methods
A history — how the methods developed over 2,000 years
A diagnosis — what organizational and market logics are currently driving the church

By the end, participants should be able to distinguish between what the church must do, what the church has historically invented to do it, and what the church has absorbed from consumer culture.

title: Session 3
text:
1. Teaching — The Framework (0:10–0:30)






Note



🗒️ Facilitator note: Write these three words on a whiteboard — PURPOSE, FUNCTIONS, METHODS — with space under each. Do not fill them in. Let the group populate them first. Your job is to ask questions and write what they say.



The three levels
Ask the group:

“Why does the church exist? Not what it does — why does it exist?“

Write their answers. Refine toward something like:






Important



PURPOSE — Why does the church exist?
To become and display God’s redeemed people in Christ, and to participate in God’s mission in the world.


Then ask:

“If that’s why it exists — what does it therefore need to do?“

Write their answers. They will generate most of this list:






Tip



FUNCTIONS — What must the church therefore do?
Worship · Teach · Form disciples · Pray · Share meals and communion · Care for those in need · Love one another · Exercise gifts · Reconcile · Evangelize · Serve · Send


Then ask:

“How does a specific church, in a specific time and place, actually accomplish those things?“







Tip



METHODS — How do we currently do those things?
Sermons · Buildings · Sunday school · Small groups · Worship bands · Youth ministry · Staff · Programs · Sunday services · Mission trips · Websites · Budgets


Then name the key principle:






Important



Purposes are enduring. Functions flow from the purposes. Methods are contextual — they shift with time, culture, and circumstance.
The problem comes when we confuse a method with a function, or a function with the purpose itself.





The purpose question in depth
The New Testament never gives a neat mission statement. You have to synthesize it. Here is one way to organize it:







Purpose
Key text




Glorify and display God
“Through the church, the manifold wisdom of God should be made known…” — Eph. 3:10


Make disciples
“Go therefore and make disciples of all nations…teaching them to obey everything I commanded.” — Matt. 28:19–20


Form people into Christlikeness
“…until we all attain…to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” — Eph. 4:13


Create a new kind of human community
“By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.” — John 13:35


Embody reconciliation
“He…has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility.” — Eph. 2:14


Bear witness to God’s kingdom
The Acts 2:42–47 community — teaching, fellowship, meals, generosity, prayer, witness


Participate in God’s mission
“God…gave us the ministry of reconciliation…We are therefore Christ’s ambassadors.” — 2 Cor. 5:18–20









Note



🗒️ Facilitator note: You do not need to work through all seven. Choose two or three that will resonate most with your group and spend time on those. The goal is to establish that the church’s purpose is richer and harder to measure than attendance, giving, or program quality.

title: Session 3
text:
3. Teaching — How the Methods Developed (1:05–1:30)






Note



🗒️ Facilitator note: Present this as a story, not a lecture. Pause after each major shift and ask: “Why do you think this happened? What problem was being solved?” Most of these changes happened for understandable reasons. The question is not “who ruined the church?” It is “what happens when solutions accumulate for 2,000 years?”



The broad arc







Era
What the church looked like




1st century
Jesus movement → household communities


2nd–3rd centuries
Increasing institutionalization: bishops, clergy, liturgy


4th century
Constantine + basilicas + professional clergy


Medieval
Sacramental church + cathedral + priesthood


Reformation
Recovery of Scripture + pulpit elevated + sermon central


Revivalism (1700s–1900s)
Preacher / audience model intensified


American voluntary church
Consumer choice + denominational competition


Modern evangelical church
Market-driven + programmatic + campus-based





One example traced in depth: the sermon
The sermon is a useful case study because it shows clearly how a method develops, becomes central, and eventually defines “church” in people’s minds.







Period
What preaching looked like




AD 30–100
Apostolic proclamation + teaching + prophecy + participatory gatherings. “When you come together, each of you has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation…” (1 Cor. 14:26)


AD 100–200
Recognizable homily emerging. Justin Martyr (c. AD 150): Scripture reading, then the president “verbally instructs and exhorts”


AD 200–300
Regular expository preaching established. Origen delivers systematic homilies on biblical books


AD 300–500
Professional clergy preach lengthy sermons to large congregations. Chrysostom — “golden-mouthed” — famous for extended biblical series


Medieval
Sermons continue but Eucharist / Mass dominates worship


1500s Reformation
Pulpit becomes visually dominant. Scripture exposition and sermon become center of Protestant worship


1700s–1900s
Revivalism further develops preacher / audience model


1900s–today
Modern evangelical: worship music + 30–45 minute sermon as the primary product









Important



The most defensible conclusion:
Preaching is ancient and thoroughly Christian.
Sermon-centered worship — where the extended monologue by a professional pastor becomes the organizing center of the weekly gathering — is much later.
The question worth asking: “How did one particular form of teaching come to dominate the gathering so completely that many Christians now instinctively think that is what ‘church’ is?“





The same pattern applies to other elements
The word “pastor”
In many American churches: “the pastor” = primary preacher + CEO + organizational leader + spiritual authority + public face.
That is not an obvious New Testament category.
Poimēn (shepherd/pastor) appears as a ministry term in Ephesians 4:11. But the far more common NT leadership language is elder (presbyteros) and overseer (episkopos), generally in the plural.
The development:
elders among the congregation → clergy offices → priest / bishop → Reformation minister → professional pastor → modern senior pastor
The building
The earliest Christians met in homes for several centuries. By the third century, adapted buildings appear (Dura-Europos, c. AD 240). After Constantine, large basilicas become Christian worship spaces — and architecture begins changing people’s understanding of church.
Instead of “The church is gathering at Lydia’s house” you increasingly get “The Christians are gathering at the basilica.”
Eventually the building itself gets called “the church.” Language naturally evolves — but it can subtly change theology.

Tip



Discussion questions:

Which column feels more familiar from your church experience? Not which one you prefer — which one you have actually encountered.
A church can unconsciously operate this feedback loop: produces religious experiences → attendees consume them → successful churches attract more consumers → revenue funds better programs → better programs attract more consumers. Have you experienced that? What did it feel like?
Some of the discomfort people feel with church may not be rejection of the church at all. It may be grief over the distance between the church they long for and the church they have experienced. Does that distinction land for anyone?
What would a church look like that genuinely operated by the community column rather than the organizational column? Have you seen it? Is it realistic?

title: Session 3
text:
Close (1:50–2:00)

“We’ve now established what the church is, what it’s for, and how we got from the New Testament to now. The next sessions get harder — we’re going to talk about authority, about harm, and about how to tell the difference between the two.
But before we do, I want to name something. The cynicism a lot of us carry about the church is not just disappointment. It’s often a sign that we knew — or hoped — the church was supposed to be something more than it has been. That intuition is worth taking seriously.”







Tip



Seed question for the week:
Think about your current or most recent church experience. Using the Purpose → Functions → Methods framework:

What methods did that church prioritize most?
What functions did those methods actually serve?
And underneath it all — what purpose did the church seem to be organized around?

Were those three things aligned?

title: Session 3
text:
Printable Participant Handout


📄 Participant Handout — Session 3

The Cynic’s Guide to Church · Session 3 · Purpose, Functions, and Methods


The framework
PURPOSE — Why does the church exist?
To become and display God’s redeemed people in Christ, and to participate in God’s mission in the world.
FUNCTIONS — What must the church therefore do?
Worship · Teach · Form disciples · Pray · Share Lord’s Supper · Care for need · Love one another · Exercise gifts · Reconcile · Evangelize · Serve · Send
METHODS — How do we accomplish those things here and now?
Sermons · Buildings · Sunday school · Small groups · Worship bands · Youth ministry · Staff · Programs · Sunday services · Mission trips



The key principle

Purposes are enduring. Functions flow from the purposes. Methods are contextual.
The danger comes when we confuse a method with a function, or a function with the purpose itself.




Why does the church exist? Seven purposes



Purpose
Key text




Glorify and display God
Eph. 3:10, 21


Make disciples
Matt. 28:19–20


Form people into Christlikeness
Eph. 4:11–13


Create a new kind of human community
John 13:35


Embody reconciliation
Eph. 2:14–15


Bear witness to God’s kingdom
Acts 2:42–47


Participate in God’s mission
2 Cor. 5:18–20






The three buckets








Bucket 1 — NT core
Bucket 2 — Historical tool
Bucket 3 — Modern consumer layer




Gathering, teaching, prayer, Lord’s Supper, baptism, singing, giving, care for poor, fellowship, accountability, evangelism, gifts, elders, deacons, discipline
Building, sermon, Sunday morning, seminary clergy, denominations, Sunday school, full-time pastor, children’s ministry, worship band
Multiple services, branding, marketing, attraction-oriented services, professional production, attendance metrics, pastor as CEO, congregation as audience



“Not commanded” does not mean “bad.” The issue is what happens when a method becomes our definition of church.

The sermon — from participatory to monologue







Period
What it looked like




AD 30–100
Participatory gatherings. “Each of you has a hymn, a lesson…” (1 Cor. 14:26)


AD 100–300
Homily emerging; expository preaching established


AD 300–500
Professional clergy preach to large congregations


Reformation
Pulpit dominant; sermon becomes center of Protestant worship

Preacher / audience model intensified


Today
Worship music + 30–45 minute sermon as principal product



Preaching is ancient and thoroughly Christian. Sermon-centered worship is much later.

Hosting on GitHub Pages
This site is built with Quarto and hosted free on GitHub Pages.

Initial setup

Create a GitHub account if you don’t have one
Create a new repository named cynics-guide-to-church (or similar)
Upload all files from this project
In repository Settings → Pages → Source: select Deploy from branch → main → /docs
Your site will be live at https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/cynics-guide-to-church



Updating the site
To rebuild after making changes:
quarto render
Then commit and push the updated docs/ folder to GitHub.


Updating the _quarto.yml
Replace YOUR-USERNAME in _quarto.yml with your actual GitHub username once the repo is created.
